LESSON 27 OF 106·Cryptography Essentials

Symmetric Encryption and Key Distribution

How one shared key delivers confidentiality, why modes and nonces matter, and the distribution problem that public-key techniques were invented to solve.

Foundation13 min
Why this matters

Symmetric encryption uses one shared key to both encrypt and decrypt. It is fast and strong, which is why nearly all data encryption is symmetric. The hard part has always been sharing the key safely.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • The same key encrypts and decrypts, so both parties must hold it, and anyone holding it can both read and forge.
  • Modern authenticated encryption combines a cipher and a MAC, so a message is both confidential and tamper-evident in one construction.
  • Nonce or initialisation vector values must never repeat under the same key, because repetition leaks information.
  • Counter mode is efficient and parallelisable, which is why it is widely used once the nonce is handled correctly.
  • Key distribution is solved today by public-key cryptography: the shared key is negotiated, and the symmetric key does the actual work.

The background

  • Block ciphers replaced stream ciphers and hand-rolled designs once block ciphers proved fast enough for most uses.
  • Stream ciphers such as RC4 were ubiquitous for decades and were deprecated once practical attacks surfaced.
  • The transition to authenticated encryption fixed a long-standing pattern where encryption and integrity were bolted together and often one was missing.
  • Nonce misuse in widely used libraries has caused repeated real breaches, which is why the risk is now treated as a design failure rather than a bug.

Real-world examples

  • A nonce reused with the same key in a widely used library made a large amount of traffic decryptable, and it took years to rotate everything.
  • A scheme that encrypts but does not authenticate lets an attacker modify ciphertext, so an application must verify before acting on it.
  • Storing a symmetric key next to the data it protects provides no real confidentiality if the same storage is compromised.

What to look for

  • Check whether the scheme provides integrity as well as confidentiality, because one alone is rarely enough.
  • Look for nonce or initialisation vector generation and confirm it cannot repeat.
  • Check where the key is stored and who can read it.
  • Notice any custom cipher or mode, which is a finding on its own.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Open OverTheWire resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Use an authenticated encryption mode from a standard library rather than combining primitives yourself.
  • Derive keys with a key derivation function, not by hashing a passphrase directly.
  • Never reuse a nonce with the same key, and prefer constructions that fail safely if one might repeat.
  • Store keys in a dedicated secret store with restricted access, and separate them from the data they protect.
  • Plan for key rotation before you need it, and confirm the rotated key actually replaces the old one.
